catalog_quote: Most conspicuous among the many developments which characterize Northern Paman reflection of Proto Paman is the reduction of Initial syllables (*CV1) by loss of initial consonants (*C1) and loss or other reduction of immediately following vowels (*V1). Associated with initial reduction, and at least partially responsible for it is a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable (*CV2) in Paman stems. In all Northern Paman languages, except Uraði and its sister dialects, *C1 was lost invariably. Even in Uraði the prevailing tendency has been toward initial loss, although *C1 is sometimes positively reflected in that language. Short *V1 was lost in some languages, retained in others, and metathesized in still others. Long *V1 was shortened in all. ... [p.179, stated for Linngithigh only] Word stress in Linŋit̪iɣ [= Linngithigh] is predictable: the first vowel which is preceded by a consonant is stressed. Accordingly, the first vowel is stressed in words beginning in a consonant or cluster ... but the second vowel in words which begin in a vowel

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: is a symlink to MB, 202 pp., archive.org micro_IA41153350_0264, ERIC ED 010 364). I rendered pp.170-171 and read the page scan: AL 8(2) p.167 bottom to p.168 top carries exactly the quoted passage ('Most conspicuous among the many developments which characterize Northern Paman reflection of Proto Paman is the reduction of Initial syllables (*CV1) by loss of initial consonants (*C1) and loss o[f/r] other reduction of immediately following vowels (*V1). Associated with initial reduction, and at least partially responsible for it is a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable (*CV2) in Paman stems. In all Northern Paman languages,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: What the source states (first-hand, Hale's own 1960 field sample which includes Yinwum, but phrased for the Northern Paman subgroup as a whole and diachronically): primary stress is non-contrastive ('a strictly phonetic feature') and sits on the syllable continuing Proto-Paman *CV2, i.e. it moved off the old initial syllable, whose *C1 Yinwum lost invariably and whose *V1 Yinwum sometimes lost (lin 'mouth', mpi- 'give', me- 'MM') and sometimes kept (ika 'spear', aji 'food', iyi 'nose', ata 'crow'). INFERENCE, not stated for Yinwum: in surface terms that puts stress on the first syllable of consonant-initial words and the second syllable of vowel-initial words, the 'first vowel preceded by a consonant' rule Hale states explicitly only for Linngithigh (same paper p.179). No Yinwum-specific synchronic stress sentence was found in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Only Uradhi and its sister dialects are excepted, and only with respect to *C1 loss, not the stress shift.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about (Proto-)Paman stems / the word; diachronic framing; subgroup-level (Northern Paman), not a description of Yinwum citation forms. Hale's Yinwum data were elicited from one informant (Tiktik) via Ngkoth (Nash 2001, AIATSIS MS 882(4)).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is made for the Northern Paman subgroup as a whole (Glottolog nort2758 'Northern Pama'), by the fieldworker whose 1960 sample includes Yinwum (yinw1236 = AUSTLANG Y29 = ISO yxm; Hale's informant Tiktik, elicited via Ngkoth; probable other dialect Njuwadhai per Sutton 2021). It is not a Yinwum-specific synchronic rule; the surface locus (first onsetful syllable) is an inference from Hale's Yinwum forms plus his explicit Linngithigh rule, and should be flagged as such if catalogued.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (symlink to the copy consulted; the PDF's metadata: 18 pp, ProQuest/UH Press scan, no text: extracted text of p.9 returns 1 byte). Rendered p.9 (= OL 3(2) p.256) and read the page scan: the quoted paragraph opens section 2 exactly as quoted ('Most conspicuous among the many developments.. is a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable.. in Paman stems.'). Minor difference only: the page prints the symbols as *CV1 / *C1 / *V1 / *CV2 (subscript on V only), the compiler wrote *C1V1 and *C2V2. The saved scanned (18 page markers) read in full; a full-text search for stress/accent|accent|prominen|intonat|tone|pitch finds only the scanned…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog row for Yinwum is 'segmental' with an empty rule; the existing statement (Hale 1966, pp.167-168) is the same Northern-Paman-wide sentence in a slightly revised wording ('loss or other reduction'; the 1966 appendix is the expanded version of this 1964 report). Hale 1964 p.256 is thus the earliest printed carrier of the 'stress shifted from initial to second syllable' statement that Blevins 2001:484,488 cites as 'Hale (1964, 1976a)' for Yinwum. It agrees with the existing statement's placement and adds the qualification that stress is 'a strictly phonetic feature' (non-contrastive); it does not give a Yinwum-specific synchronic stress rule, so it refines (family-level, diachronic)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: A Northern-Paman-wide historical statement, not a Yinwum-specific synchronic rule: in the Paman stems inherited by the Northern Paman languages (Yinwum is subgroup (C) of the 13-variety sample, p.252), primary stress shifted from the initial to the second syllable, and this shift is held partly responsible for the loss of the initial consonant and reduction of the first vowel. Read synchronically, stress in the modern languages falls on what was the second syllable of the proto-stem, i.e. the first surviving full syllable after initial reduction (Linngithigh *pama > ma, Yinwum *tYalan > lin 'mouth'); Hale calls stress 'a strictly phonetic feature', i.e. non-contrastive. The Yinwum-specific paragraphs (pp.256-257 prenasalised stops from initial nasals; p.259 *NS reduction and vowel umlaut; p.261 discontinuous reflexes of long *V1, e.g. *nYi:rri > iyi 'nose', *yi:pa(r) > ipya-t 'south') say nothing further about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. For the associated initial reduction: Uradhi (not Yinwum) sometimes keeps *C1 (p.256); in Yinwum both *C1 and short *V1 are lost, with metathesis in some languages (pp.260-261).
new_statements.identity_note: Hale's Yinwum is the language 'spoken south of Moreton on the Batavia River and west to Cox Creek' (p.253, term cp. /yin/ 'this'; McConnel 1939), one informant sample obtained in 1960 at Weipa/Aurukun; this is yinw1236 (AUSTLANG Y29). The stress statement itself is made for Northern Paman (and 'Paman stems') collectively, not for the Yinwum variety alone.
